title_page_text: ENHANCING R&D CAPACITY IN GREATER MANCHESTER'S CREATIVE TECHNOLOGY SECTOR
Executive Summary - Strategic Context
Understanding Innovation Flows and Building Capacity

Greater Manchester's creative technology R&D ecosystem currently operates as a collection of isolated towers. MediaCity rises in one location, Manchester and Man Met universities in the Oxford Road corridor, the Northern Quarter clusters in another, whilst production assets spread outward from the airport. Yet these concentrations of capability remain functionally disconnected, lacking the essential bridges that enable innovation flow and knowledge transfer.

This isolation manifests most clearly in our analysis of and engagement with national R&D funding programmes. Despite significant creative technology capability, Greater Manchester has failed in three successive attempts to secure clusters funding. This reflects a fundamental challenge: we don't understand how innovation actually moves through our ecosystem.
Current Innovation Reality

The contrast in innovation success tells a compelling story. At dock10, collaboration with the University of York drives genuine advancement in AI-driven lighting systems, creating both commercial advantage and environmental benefit through reduced energy consumption. Yet keyword analysis of UKRI Collaborative R&D projects reveals only 14 SME-led creative technology projects in the period 2018-2024. This disconnect between academic work and market need reflects a broader pattern: local universities continue to pursue theoretical research with limited market application, exemplified by Manchester Metropolitan University's repeated failures to secure funding for an R&D cluster in screen, real time and creative technologies. The broader innovation landscape, particularly around creative technology, remains largely unmapped.

The ecosystem stands at a critical juncture. The closure of Pathway XR, alongside other market pressures and reports of skills gaps and shortages, highlights both challenges and opportunities in building sustainable R&D capacity. This proposal delivers a focused, actionable framework to give creative employers the confidence to recruit, seek access to finance, increase innovation absorption and build resilient growth.
Phase 1: Understanding Innovation Flows

The challenge extends beyond simple mapping. In creative technology, innovation often flows through informal networks and collaborative relationships that resist traditional measurement. These connections - the bridges between our towers - frequently comprise freelance specialists and micro-businesses moving between projects and organisations.

Feedback from evaluation of the first round of AHRC Creative Industries Clusters, however, could not identify a relationship between the presence of freelancers in the creative cluster and evidence of successful collaborative R&D by creative SMEs. This is understandable: there was no systematic attempt made to measure the scale and significance of the freelance workforce within those geographies. This reflects a national picture where national statistics capture only statistical projections of PAYE employment, determined both by Standard Industrial Classifications (SIC codes) of which are widely held to underrepresent new and emerging technologies and a weighting of a sample whose representativeness is questioned.

This sits oddly with a body of academic literature which asserts that workforce movements create vital pathways for knowledge transfer and innovation diffusion. Without understanding these patterns, we cannot effectively support or enhance them. This gap in understanding directly impacts the ability of Manchester’s creative technology SMEs to access national R&D funding and build sustainable innovation capacity. Therefore, our proposal builds on a proven bespoke methodology to measure the freelance creative workforce and introduces new elements to help us analyse trends in adoption of creative technology skills. Together, this will demonstrate whether there is a correlation between increasing demand for creative tech skills and ‘hotspots’ within the existing ecosystem, which we can then test further through engagement and consultation to establish causality, including measuring where there is a measurable increase in absorptive capacity for innovation and identifying skills gaps and shortages which may be blocking innovation flows.
Strategic Context
Recent developments highlight both the urgency and opportunity in addressing this challenge:

Understanding and enhancing these innovation flows requires careful examination of how different parts of our ecosystem currently interact. This goes beyond simple sector mapping to understand the actual mechanisms of innovation transfer and absorption.

title_page_text: IV Key Insights
Challenges in University-Business Collaboration
There's a widespread issue across universities (not just Salford) in engaging with businesses meaningfully.
Difficulty in identifying researchers doing relevant work that businesses care about.
Some personal connections exist, but institutional engagement remains weak.

title_page_text: Social Network Analysis of MITIH Database Organisations
1.1 Overview

To construct an accurate visual depiction of the possible connections between organisations in Manchester’s createch ecosystem, the research has utilised a social network analysis (SNA) methodology to map workforce movement between 129 GM companies derived from MITIH datasets.

At its core, SNA provides a method for displaying and analysing relational data through the mapping of “nodes” (the individual actors within a network), connected by “edges” (the ties that connect nodes to one another). Mapping connections in this way offers a means of quantitively capturing the overall structure of actors within a network. In this research context, the nodes are createch organisations, and an edge is drawn between any two nodes if evidence is found of employee movement between them. The result is a a “map” of inter-connected organisations, representing a visual eco-system (see fig 1 for the graph and fig 2 for a further breakdown of its properties).
1.2 Research Strengths
Visually depicting the createch ecosystem presents three primary opportunities for further insight:
Identification of strong instances of connection between a group of organisations.
Identification of missing, weak or potential connections between organisations.
Stimulus for the development of strategies to reduce uncertainties and resource-waste, whilst encouraging judicious and active approaches to improving further collaboration and knowledge-sharing.

The first two opportunities should act as starting points for further research. If a node is found to have strong connections to other nodes, it is prudent to consider the properties of the organisations represented. Factors such as the type of work completed, the company size and its connections to other nodes within the network should help createch org’s build up their own index of potential collaborators. Likewise, whilst organisations should capitalise on areas of strength, time should be taken to reinforce porous elements of the network structure and the properties of poorly connected nodes should be interrogated.
The third opportunity refers to the fundamental principle on which the social network analysis portion of the research is based:

All organisations exist within a network of other organisations. Viewing yourself not as an individual, but as a member of an inter-connected network allows you to view your actions as they reverberate throughout the wider network structure and to allocate resources and broker relationships with greater strategic insight.
Research Limitations

Whilst the outcome of the SNA remains a useful proof-of-concept for the strengths of network visualisation, the nature of the data from which the network was derived limits the scope of analysis. The findings of this research must therefore be caveated by the following: workforce movement through the createch ecosystem does not directly demonstrate innovation flow. Instead, companies should use the information provided as a starting point with a view to gaining further information about their fellow network participants, only then can tangible and real-time pathways for innovation flow be realised.

title_page_text: Glossary

Createch: The intersection of creative industries and technology, specifically referring to businesses and professionals working across digital creative sectors including animation, audio/music production, studio production, immersive technologies (XR/VR/AR), and related digital support services.

Innovation Hub: A physical location, organisation, or programme specifically designed to concentrate innovation activities, resources, and talent. Innovation hubs typically provide some combination of:
Physical workspace and specialised facilities/equipment
Access to funding, investment, and business development support
Networking and collaboration opportunities
Mentorship, expertise, and knowledge sharing
Structured programmes (accelerators, incubators) to support new ventures or projects

Innovation hubs in the creative technology context often include production facilities, testing environments, demonstration spaces, and collaborative work areas. While traditional innovation hubs often operate as centralised entities with a single physical location and management structure, the report advocates for a more distributed "federated hub" model (see below) that better suits the mesh-based approach to creative technology innovation. In Greater Manchester's creative ecosystem, examples include components of MediaCity, HOST and university-based hubs like SODA. The report suggests these hubs could be more effective by embedding mesh enabler roles (see below) and adopting practices that facilitate broader cross-sector collaboration rather than operating primarily within defined sectoral boundaries.

Federated Hubs: A network of physical and/or virtual spaces distributed across Greater Manchester that serve as collaboration centres for creative technology sectors. Unlike centralised innovation hubs, federated hubs operate with some independence while maintaining connections and shared resources with each other, enabling localised collaboration while contributing to the broader ecosystem.

Mesh/Network Approach: A strategic framework that prioritises connections, relationships, and collaboration infrastructure over traditional sector-based or output-focused models. This approach views creative technology as an interconnected system rather than distinct vertical sectors.

Mesh Enabler Roles: Professional positions specifically designed to facilitate connection, translation, and collaboration between different creative sectors, organisations, programmes/projects and disciplines. Examples include technical producers, project coordinators, and workflow specialists who can bridge between animation, audio, and studio production teams.

Mesh Fluency: The ability to work effectively across different creative disciplines, technical systems, and organisational cultures. This includes communication skills, project management capabilities, and understanding of various production pipelines.

Mesh Infrastructure: The combination of people, processes, platforms, programmes, projects and physical spaces that enable effective collaboration across organisational and sectoral boundaries in the creative technology ecosystem.

Zebra Organisations: Values-led businesses that prioritise sustainable growth and ethical practices over rapid scaling or exit strategies (contrasted with "unicorn" startups). These organisations often serve critical roles in ecosystem stability through relationship building, skills anchoring, and providing informal infrastructure.

title_page_text: Herefordshire Cultural Strategy 2025-2030
Executive Summary

Herefordshire stands at a pivotal moment in its cultural development. Building on five years of significant progress toward achieving the aims of the previous cultural strategy, led by the Herefordshire Cultural Partnership (HCP), the revised strategy sets out an ambitious yet practical vision for how culture can drive economic growth, enhance wellbeing, and strengthen communities across our distinctively  rural county.

This strategy has been developed by the Herefordshire Cultural Partnership in collaboration with Herefordshire Council and a wide range of stakeholders. It builds on the achievements of the 2019-2024 Cultural Strategy while responding to the changing context for cultural development locally, regionally, and nationally.
The Rural Context: Challenges and Opportunities
Herefordshire's rurality presents both unique challenges and distinctive opportunities for cultural development:

Geographic Dispersion: As one of England's most sparsely populated counties, Herefordshire faces significant challenges in cultural provision, with communities separated by considerable distances and limited public transport
Seasonal Disruption: Environmental factors, including flooding, regularly impact cultural participation and delivery, requiring adaptive approaches to programming and engagement
Digital Connectivity: Variable broadband access creates barriers to digital cultural engagement in rural areas, while also offering opportunities for innovative solutions

title_page_text: From local mesh to national AI strategy: a tale of two UK screen sector reports

Two significant recent reports address the impact of AI on the UK screen sector. At first glance, they seem to operate in different worlds. The Fifth Sector’s ‘MITIH Createch Ecosystem Report’ for Salford City Council is a granular, data-rich deep dive into the structural health of Greater Manchester's (GM) animation, audio, and studio production sectors. The CoSTAR Foresight Lab's 'AI in the Screen Sector' report is a high-level, national analysis of the opportunities and threats posed by one single, transformative technology: generative AI.

Reading them in isolation provides valuable insight. Reading them together, however, reveals a powerful, unified narrative about the future of the UK's creative economy. They are not two separate stories, but two sides of the same coin. One provides the ground truth; the other provides the strategic context.
Here’s how they correspond, complement, and create a productive tension with one another.
Where the reports align: a shared diagnosis
Despite their different scopes, both reports arrive at strikingly similar conclusions about the state of the screen industries.
The skills mismatch is real
The Fifth Sector report highlights that the most in-demand skills are no longer purely technical, but collaborative and operational:
"Communication, agile methodology, project management, and content creation top the charts."

The CoSTAR report echoes this, noting that to survive the AI wave, the sector must "develop the sector to build skills complementary to AI," implicitly valuing human-centric abilities that machines cannot replicate.
A disconnect between policy and reality

The Fifth Sector report unpicks the risks in the current policy approach to AI, immersive production and film and television, highlighting "Policy Assumptions about Innovation Flows vs Evidence-Backed Reality." It argues that funders and policymakers are often working from an outdated playbook. The CoSTAR report makes the same point through its "iceberg" metaphor, explaining that while public examples of AI use are few, there is a huge amount of experimentation happening "beneath the surface," away from the eyes of strategists.
The future of creative work is precarious

Both reports sound a warning. The Fifth Sector report identifies the audio sector as "drifting toward obsolescence" and animation as "active but isolated," making it vulnerable. The CoSTAR report notes that AI automation threatens entry-level jobs, potentially cutting off the talent pipeline, and that creators risk significant revenue loss.

title_page_text: Executive Summary
Future-Proofing the UK Screen Sector:
Strategic Investment for Resilience and Talent Development
Prepared for the British Screen Forum by Iain Bennett of The Fifth Sector and Jon Bains of Obsolete
August 2025
Key findings and their implications for UK Screen

The UK screen sector, encompassing film, television, broadcasting, and digital content, is a cornerstone of the nation’s creative economy, celebrated for its innovation and global reach. However, recent in-depth analysis of Greater Manchester's screen production sector, focused on animation, audio, and studio production, revealed systemic fragilities and overlooked opportunities that hold profound implications for the entire national screen landscape. Our report, grounded in robust data and extensive stakeholder consultation, highlights that the long-term health and global competitiveness of the UK screen sector are intrinsically linked to the resilience and interconnectedness of a set of foundational capabilities, requiring a re-evaluation of macro-level investment strategies.
1.1	Fragmented networks and innovation bottlenecks

Our research indicates a dense but highly fragmented creative and digital network, with a strikingly low level of active organisational links. Animation clusters, despite their internal strength, remain isolated, limiting innovation and increasing vulnerability to dwindling commissions from UK public service broadcasters. This fragmentation hinders the rapid formation of multidisciplinary teams essential for new screen content formats (e.g., virtual production, interactive storytelling). For the UK screen sector, this translates to a slower pace of innovation and reduced capacity to leverage emerging technologies effectively.
1.2	Undervalued foundational infrastructure and skills

Studio production and audio roles, while consistently in demand and critical to content delivery, are largely invisible in existing policy frameworks and innovation strategies. This leads to chronic underfunding of a "hidden infrastructure" of technical craft and freelance talent. This translates to a brittle production backbone, risking the loss of crucial operational capabilities essential for efficient and high-quality content delivery across film, TV, and digital platforms.
1.3	Shifting talent demands and misaligned pipelines

The job market reveals a significant shift towards "mesh fluency" – the ability to collaborate, communicate, and prototype in mixed teams – which gains increasing relevance with increased adoption of AI, even as traditional programming languages decline. A "brain drain" of top talent to London exacerbates regional skills gaps, as universities and training providers often fail to adequately prepare graduates for hybrid, cross-disciplinary production environments. Without recalibration, the sector risks a persistent shortage of adaptable, collaborative professionals, impacting future production capacity and quality.
1.4	The critical role of "Zebra" organisations

The screen sector is quietly sustained by "Zebra" organisations – values-led SMEs prioritising sustainability and collaboration in creation of new content and services. These entities act as vital trust brokers and provide informal delivery infrastructure, enabling cross-sector prototypes. Despite their fundamental role in stabilising the production environment, they struggle to attract support from public sector funding models focused on high-growth metrics. Neglecting these organisations undermines the very fabric of the UK screen sector's agile, independent production base, risking a loss of cultural continuity and regional anchoring.

title_page_text: MITIH Createch Ecosystem Report: Stakeholder-Aligned Summary
A Framework for Greater Manchester's Creative Sector Growth
Executive Summary

Greater Manchester possesses significant creative and digital sector capacity across animation, audio, and studio production. This analysis identifies opportunities to strengthen connectivity between these capabilities, enhance talent development, and position the region for sustainable growth in an evolving media landscape.
Key Findings:

1. Convergence Opportunity Across Sub-Sectors
Animation, audio, and studio production share underlying skills and capacity that are currently underutilised. Emerging demand patterns—particularly in immersive technologies, advertising, and digital content—reveal significant opportunities for cross-sector collaboration. These sub-sectors are not competing for the same resources; rather, they represent complementary capabilities that can be more effectively deployed when connected.

2. Skills Alignment and Talent Pipeline Development
The labour market is shifting toward collaborative, adaptive capabilities: communication, project management, and cross-disciplinary fluency now rank alongside technical skills. Current educational and training pathways, structured around legacy sector verticals, do not adequately prepare talent for these hybrid environments. Universities and training providers have an opportunity to co-design curricula that embed practical, cross-sector collaboration from the outset.

3. Infrastructure Access and Affordability
A significant gap exists between high-cost commercial facilities (which require substantial investment to access) and university-based resources (which face procurement and access constraints). Emerging opportunities exist to create shared, accessible infrastructure that serves multiple sectors and enables SMEs and early-stage practitioners to access tools and expertise close to the point of need.

4. The Role of Values-Led Organisations
Sustainable, community-aligned organisations play a critical stabilising role in the ecosystem, acting as trust brokers and enabling cross-sector prototypes. These organisations require different support models than high-growth ventures and deserve recognition as strategic assets rather than peripheral players.

5. Immersive as an Integration Layer
Immersive technologies (VR/XR) are not speculative future opportunities but practical, current integration points. Immersive projects inherently require animation, audio, and studio production expertise working in concert. This convergence offers a fundable, commercially viable pathway for cross-sector collaboration.
Strategic Opportunities for Cluster Development:

Sub-Sector Engagement: Convene animation, audio, and studio production communities separately around their specific opportunities and challenges. This approach allows each sub-sector to articulate its distinct needs while revealing shared infrastructure and skills requirements.

Shared Infrastructure Models: Develop accessible, jointly-funded facilities and platforms that serve multiple sectors, reducing barriers to entry for SMEs and enabling talent mobility across sub-sectors.

University-Industry Co-Investment: Create mechanisms for universities and industry to jointly invest in shared infrastructure, programmes, and talent development, breaking down institutional silos and procurement barriers.
Immersive as a Testbed: Use immersive technology projects as a practical proving ground for cross-sector collaboration, demonstrating commercial viability and building collaborative muscle memory.

title_page_text: Greater Manchester Immersive Production
Investment Recommendations: Building on Research Findings
Prepared for Greater Manchester Combined Authority and Salford City Council October 2025
Executive Summary

The Fifth Sector's research commissioned by MITIH demonstrates that Greater Manchester possesses genuine operational capability in immersive production. Realtime's Virtual Production department proves that cross- sector integration between animation, audio, and studio production functions as a commercially viable business model. The research identiﬁes skilled workforce, established anchor organisations, and speciﬁc infrastructure opportunities that could support cluster expansion.

These ﬁndings reveal capability and opportunity. However, capability does not guarantee sustainable investment outcomes without validated market demand. This recommendations document proposes a risk-managed investment sequence that builds on research-validated operational strengths while ensuring market fundamentals support expansion before committing substantial public funds.

The core recommendation is straightforward: invest £40,000-60,000 in systematic demand validation before proceeding with training expansion or major infrastructure development. This modest upfront analysis addresses three critical questions the ecosystem research could not answer within its scope, and prevents potential losses exceeding £500,000 if market timing proves unfavourable.
What the Research Established

The MITIH research provides comprehensive documentation of Greater Manchester's immersive production ecosystem as it exists today, based on three months of direct evidence collection in early 2025. Five key ﬁndings emerge:

Immersive production as convergence space: Realtime's Virtual Production department demonstrates that animation, audio, and studio production can integrate as a single commercial operation delivering paid work. Job market data shows 3,847 immersive-related postings between 2020-2024, with signiﬁcant overlap between animation skills (34% of postings), audio expertise (28%), and studio production experience (41%) within the same roles.

Employer demand shifting toward collaboration: Analysis of 51,419 postings requesting communication skills (up 15%), 37,229 requesting agile methodology (up 38%), and 16,348 requesting project management (up 33%) contrasts with declining technical specialisation demands like JavaScript (down 74%) and Azure (down 61%). Employers seek integration ﬂuency across disciplines, not narrow technical depth.
Infrastructure barriers at modest cost thresholds: Speciﬁc equipment access constraints—such as the

£17,000 portable EEG system—prevent SME participation in collaborative R&D. Only 26 UKRI awards totalling £2.01 million reached Greater Manchester creative ﬁrms between 2019-2024, reﬂecting mechanism mismatch rather than absence of fundable ideas.

Microbusinesses as ecosystem stabilisers: Creative and digital microbusinesses provide essential cross-sector bridging and collaboration facilitation. Social network analysis conﬁrms their structural importance despite modest commercial scale. Traditional high-growth funding mechanisms actively work against these stabilising organisations.

Proven model replicability potential: Realtime's convergent production model is operationally demonstrated and commercially sustained, providing a template for potential expansion across additional organisations.

Strategic Opportunities for Greater Manchester
Summary prepared for Salford City Council
by Iain Bennett and Jon Bains
25 October 2025
Executive Summary

Greater Manchester’s legacy of broadcast commissioning and production established the foundation onto which MediaCity was designed to add new capacity in creation and distribution of new, digital forms of creativity. Across animation, audio, and studio production, the region possesses world-class creative capability, proven commercial success, and a track record of innovation. Yet this capability remains fragmented, underutilised and, as a consequence, at risk.

Research commissioned by MITIH and carried out by The Fifth Sector over three months in early 2025 reveals the potential for  cross-sector integration between animation, audio, and studio production functions as a commercially viable business model. The research identiﬁes skilled workforce, established anchor organisations, and speciﬁc infrastructure opportunities that could support cluster expansion.

Greater Manchester can make a strong argument to funders and investors that it is uniquely positioned to lead the UK in demonstrating how creative sectors can operate as an integrated, resilient ecosystem. Combining detailed analysis of labour market trends from 2020-2024, organisational networks, and direct engagement with sector leaders, the report identifies specific, actionable opportunities where targeted investment can unlock significant value from existing capacity.
The research points to five critical findings:

Immersive production is already functioning as a convergence space where animation, audio, and studio production naturally work together. This is not theoretical; it is happening now, commercially viable, and ready to scale.

Employer demand has fundamentally shifted from narrow technical specialisation toward collaborative, adaptive capability. Yet educational provision has not caught up. This creates both a risk and an opportunity for universities to differentiate themselves by aligning with actual employer needs.

There are structural barriers to take up of innovation funding to support collaborative R&D between University and digital and creative firms across GM. Specific, modest-cost infrastructure gaps can be addressed through targeted funding, unlocking participation from small and medium-sized businesses that currently cannot afford access to premium facilities.

The region's most essential stabilising organisations are its creative and digital microbusiness, not the broadcasters or Universities. These are not struggling businesses; they are strategic assets that enable cross-sector collaboration and innovation. The risk to the GM ecosystem lies in that fact that these SMEs are systematically underfunded. Traditional funding models designed for high-growth ventures actively work against them.

Greater Manchester can scale what is already working. Realtime's Virtual Production department demonstrates that convergence between animation, audio, and studio production is operationally viable and commercially sustainable. This model is replicable and fundable.
